entries.title: MentalHealthBench scores model replies against weighted expert-consensus rubrics
entries.summary: OpenAI released an open benchmark of synthetic mental health conversations, from everyday stress to emergencies, across adults, teens, caregivers and clinicians. Over 80 licensed experts wrote per-conversation rubric items weighted from -10 to +10, and only items that at least two of three reviewers agreed on were kept. A model grader scores replies against these rubrics, and the score can be split into ten behavior dimensions, so models with the same total can show different strengths.

lessons.point: Per-conversation rubric items carry signed weights, so harmful behavior is penalized and clinically important behavior counts more, rather than a single pass/fail.
lessons.excerpt: They each carry a weight ranging from -10 to +10: positive points reward beneficial behaviors, while negative points penalize harmful ones

lessons.point: Rubric quality control uses a simple consensus rule: keep an item only if two of three experts agree and none contradicts it.
lessons.excerpt: we only retained criteria agreed upon by at least two experts and not contradicted by a third

lessons.point: Breaking the total score into behavior dimensions reveals differences that a single headline number hides.
lessons.excerpt: Models with similar overall scores can have different strengths across these behaviors.

lessons.point: Users and experts value different things: users weight practical next steps and tone, experts weight context-gathering. The benchmark scores only the expert view.
lessons.excerpt: User perspectives highlighted qualities people value in AI support that were less emphasized in expert guidance, particularly practical next steps and tone.

entries.takeaway: For subjective, high-stakes domains, weighted per-scenario rubrics with an expert-agreement filter and dimension-level scoring give a more usable eval than a single safety pass rate.

actionable.title: Build domain evals as weighted per-scenario rubrics with an agreement filter
actionable.detail: For each eval scenario, have 3 domain reviewers write single-aspect criteria with signed weights (e.g. -10..+10); keep only criteria at least 2 agree on and none contradicts; grade with a model judge against those criteria and report per-dimension scores alongside the total, not just the headline number.

entries.title: SAFT adversarially trains only robustness-critical parameters and beats LoRA
entries.summary: Adversarial training (AT) makes neural networks robust to small adversarial input perturbations, but it is memory-heavy on large models. LoRA-based AT leaves a robustness gap compared with full-parameter AT. The authors find that adversarial gradients concentrate on a small set of "Robustness-Critical Parameters". Sparse Adversarial Fine-Tuning (SAFT) updates only those, about 5% of parameters, and the abstract says it approaches or surpasses full AT on robustness.

lessons.point: Low-rank adapters cost robustness compared with full-parameter adversarial training.
lessons.excerpt: this constraint induces a notable robustness gap relative to full-parameter AT

lessons.point: Gradient analysis suggests robustness lives in a sparse subset of weights.
lessons.excerpt: adversarial optimization is highly concentrated on a small subset of parameters

lessons.point: Updating only the salient parameters beats LoRA on both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters.
lessons.excerpt: SAFT outperforms LoRA-based methods in both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters

entries.takeaway: This is a model-training result for classic adversarial robustness and has little direct use for agent or harness builders.

actionable.title: Note as a PEFT alternative for robust fine-tuning
actionable.detail: If you adversarially fine-tune your own classifiers, such as a guardrail model, try saliency-selected sparse updates in place of LoRA and compare robust accuracy. Otherwise, no action is needed.

entries.title: Daniel Miessler argues harnesses should describe what you want, not steps
entries.summary: Daniel Miessler offers a way to remember what a harness is for: the model handles how to do the task, and the harness supplies what you want. That means your preferences, goals, context and what good looks like. He argues that harnesses which force the model through fixed steps limit it, while harnesses that describe your goals let it choose its own path. This is an opinion piece with no experiments.

lessons.point: Miessler quotes Theo's definition: a harness is the code around a model, its tools, the format for calling them, and the loop that runs them.
lessons.excerpt: The code wrapped around a model that lets it act

lessons.point: Forcing the model through fixed steps limits its results. Describing goals and preferences works better.
lessons.excerpt: Micromanaging the steps caps the model; describing what you want frees it

lessons.point: Context about the user stays valuable as models improve, even though he also says you will need the harness less.
lessons.excerpt: A smarter model does more with that context, not less.

entries.takeaway: Spend harness effort on user context and definitions of done rather than step-by-step scripts, as a heuristic, not a measured result.

actionable.title: Replace step scripts with goal, preference and done-criteria context
actionable.detail: Review your agent's system prompt and skills. Where they prescribe numbered steps, try swapping them for who the user is, how they like things done and what a finished result looks like. Compare the two versions on the same task set before adopting the change.

entries.prior_art: No direct match. Closest: the claim retest-harness-scaffolding-on-model-change and 'Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution' (ai-research). The post mostly restates the author's earlier essays.

entries.title: Survey maps how self-improving AI systems can fake gains or lose safeguards
entries.summary: A new survey defines recursive self-improvement as AI systems changing their own models, prompts, memories, tools and update mechanisms, and groups the requirements for doing it safely into four themes: genuine improvement, behavioral constraints and alignment, security and privacy, and transparency and controllability. It warns that reported gains can come from flawed evaluations, that compromised artifacts can carry into successor systems, and that changing the improvement process can invalidate earlier verification. It is a literature review with no new experiments.

lessons.point: Self-reported gains can be evaluation artifacts, and old capabilities and constraints can erode.
lessons.excerpt: Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken.

lessons.point: Compromised artifacts can carry into later versions of a self-updating system.
lessons.excerpt: Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems.

lessons.point: Changing how the system improves can void earlier verification.
lessons.excerpt: Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective.

entries.takeaway: If your agent rewrites its own prompts, memory or tools, re-verify after each change against a held-out evaluation it cannot edit.

actionable.title: Gate self-modifying agents on a frozen held-out evaluation
actionable.detail: When an agent edits its own prompts, skills, memory or tools, keep a held-out evaluation set and scoring code outside its write access, re-run it after every accepted change, and keep the previous version to roll back to.

entries.verify_note: Mostly faithful; theme list corrected to the abstract's wording, and 'no new experiments' is inferred from it being a survey.
entries.prior_art: The ledger already holds a claim that harness-evolution gains need held-out attribution; this survey restates the risk more broadly without new data.

entries.title: Titus Winters says AI raised code output and outages, not features shipped
entries.summary: In a Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Titus Winters, lead author of Software Engineering at Google, says engineers he talks to report code output up sharply, outages up about 30%, and features shipped flat. He describes Google's 2010 cleanup of a roughly 250-million-line C++ codebase done without LLMs (abstract syntax tree matching, generated edits, old and new APIs coexisting, sharded rollout, blocking the old pattern, then deletion) and Google's rule that every change carry a test. He argues AI's real value is enabling projects too ambitious to attempt before, not doing the same work faster.

lessons.point: More code output from AI does not mean more delivered value: Winters reports outages up about 30% with features shipped flat, though this is anecdote from conversations, not a measured study.
lessons.excerpt: outages are also up about 30%, while the number of features shipped is static

lessons.point: Google's pre-LLM large-scale refactor recipe was to parse code into abstract syntax trees, match exact patterns, generate edits, let old and new APIs coexist, ship by directory shard, block the old pattern, then delete it.
lessons.excerpt: ran a MapReduce over the whole codebase. The mapper parsed every build target into an abstract syntax tree

lessons.point: After Google required a test with every change, Google Search returned from quarterly to its former faster shipping cadence.
lessons.excerpt: mandated that every change was to be accompanied by a test

lessons.point: Winters argues productivity metrics that count speed on existing work miss AI's main benefit, which is making previously unrealistic projects feasible.
lessons.excerpt: He sees the real value of AI as not in repeating the same things as before at higher speed.

entries.takeaway: Judge AI-assisted engineering by outages and delivered features, not code volume, and wrap large AI rewrites in the coexist, shard and block-the-old discipline Google used before LLMs.

actionable.title: Track outages and shipped features alongside AI code output
actionable.detail: When measuring an AI coding rollout, report change-failure or outage rate and features shipped next to lines or PRs produced. For agent-driven migrations, keep old and new APIs working side by side, ship edits in directory-sized shards, add a check that blocks reintroducing the old pattern, and delete the old API only at the end.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld lessons 1, 3 and 4; lesson 2's agent-migration framing was our inference and was reworded to the recipe the source gives (novelty 22 vs 30, lower kept).
entries.prior_art: The pool's work-efficiency claim that developers misjudge AI speedups (METR's early-2025 study) already makes the point that output impressions mislead; Google's large-scale change practice is documented in the Software Engineering at Google book. The 30% outage figure is new but anecdotal.

entries.title: HybridAgent reasons in latent space and calls tools in text
entries.author: allinonai
entries.summary: HybridAgents switch between hidden-state (latent) reasoning and text-based tool interaction within one generation. A small HybridLink module handles the switch between modes, and a continuous working memory carries the mixed context across turns. Two training stages teach this behavior: HybridSFT (supervised fine-tuning) and HybridRL (reinforcement learning). Across 3 model scales and 11 benchmarks, the authors report a 10.4% performance gain, 35.5%-54.7% fewer tokens, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference and 2.7x-3.7x lower cost.
entries.takeaway: This is a model architecture and training change, not a harness technique, so it only matters if you train or serve your own open-weight agent models.

lessons.point: Pure latent reasoning has no native tool access and cannot be inspected, which is the gap the hybrid design targets.
lessons.excerpt: latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency

lessons.point: The RL stage learns when to think internally and when to emit text and actions, rather than using a fixed schedule.
lessons.excerpt: HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text

lessons.point: The reported efficiency gains are large, but they are the authors' own numbers against baselines they chose. Only the abstract was available.
lessons.excerpt: HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings

actionable.title: Track latent-reasoning agents as a future cost lever, not a current harness change
actionable.detail: If you self-host open-weight agent models, check the togethercomputer/HybridAgent release and re-run its token and latency claims on your own agent tasks before adopting it. Harnesses built on closed APIs have nothing to apply.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: every fact matches the abstract. Verifier novelty 35 (closest: Coconut-style continuous-thought work), relevance 22; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: No close pool entry. Nearby archive items cover latent-space methods for other purposes, such as activation-based fact-checking. The new claim is a single model that mixes latent thoughts with text tool calls and can still inspect those thoughts. It sits in model internals, outside the practitioner harness focus.

entries.title: Daniel Miessler frames AI work as hill-climbing against ideal-state evals
entries.summary: Daniel Miessler argues that most AI work follows one loop. You state your purpose, write down the ideal state, turn it into evals, let AI do the work, then iterate on both the output and the evals. He claims the main limit today is how clearly people say what they want, not what AI can do. The essay lists eval types, from plain code checks to repeated runs and judges tuned on your past ratings, and it has no experiments.

lessons.point: Miessler claims stating the goal clearly, not AI execution, is now the main constraint.
lessons.excerpt: the primary limitation for AI today is not its ability to build what you ask for. It's your ability to clearly articulate what you want.

lessons.point: If output passes every eval but you still dislike it, the evals need updating.
lessons.excerpt: The best way to tell if you need to update your evals is if you get a result that perfectly passes your evals, but you still don't like it for some reason.

lessons.point: Evals should include actually running the thing and repeated trials, not a single pass.
lessons.excerpt: Does it hold up every time? (running it ten times and seeing how many pass, not just once)

entries.takeaway: Treat the written ideal state as the source of your verification criteria, and update the evals whenever passing output still feels wrong.

actionable.title: Derive eval checks directly from the task's ideal-state doc
actionable.detail: For each agent task, write the ideal state as a list of checkable criteria. Mix code checks, reference comparisons, run-it-and-see tests and multi-run pass rates. Add a criterion whenever an output passes everything but is still rejected.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: lessons supported by the essay; it is opinion without experiments.
entries.prior_art: The nearest entry is Miessler's own 'Daniel Miessler argues harnesses should describe what you want, not steps' (ai-research), which makes the same ideal-state argument. The eval taxonomy restates common practice.

entries.title: Simon Willison's Claude-run review finds webframe fast but rough for scraping
entries.summary: webframe, a small Go tool by Jeff Lindsay, runs a web page or file in the operating system's own hidden web view and prints `console.log()` output to standard output. Simon Willison had Claude Opus 5.5 test it as a scraper and as a sandbox. The report finds it fast and comparable to shot-scraper for scraping, but with rough edges: CSP failures, a 0×0 viewport, hanging loads, missing HTTP metadata and limited browser controls. The captured post gives no detail on the sandbox verdict.

lessons.point: webframe runs a page like a command-line program, printing console output.
lessons.excerpt: lets you "run a web page like a program"

lessons.point: The evaluation found several practical rough edges.
lessons.excerpt: but with important rough edges including CSP failures, a 0×0 viewport, hanging loads, missing HTTP metadata, and limited browser controls.

lessons.point: It uses the system browser engine rather than bundling one.
lessons.excerpt: it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine.

entries.takeaway: webframe is a lightweight way to run page JavaScript from scripts, but do not treat it as a sandbox without your own isolation.

actionable.title: Try webframe for light page scripting, not isolation
actionable.detail: For agent or scraping tasks that just need page JavaScript output, webframe is a smaller alternative to Playwright-based tools. Run it inside your own container or VM if pages are untrusted, since the post gives no sandbox guarantees.

entries.verify_note: Matches the captured blurb; details rest on a one-line summary of the linked report.
entries.prior_art: shot-scraper and Playwright-based runners already cover this; webframe is a smaller variant built on the system web view.

entries.title: Practitioners say public AI security benchmarks only shortlist models for real work
entries.summary: Dark Reading asked vendors how they measure AI models on security work: XBOW builds its own harness and scores exploit-finding, Sonar's leaderboard ranks secure code generation, and the UK AI Security Institute tests whether models can complete a 32-step attack chain, which two models have done so far. Interviewees agree public rankings only shortlist candidates and that the harness around a model matters as much as the model. XBOW adds that harm is hard to benchmark, because one bad run after a thousand clean ones outweighs them all.

lessons.point: Public benchmarks narrow the field, but the decision needs your own evaluations.
lessons.excerpt: Public benchmarks help shortlist candidates, but the decision needs evaluations that reflect your own code and workflows.

lessons.point: The harness, not just the model, decides how well context and tools are used.
lessons.excerpt: The model supplies capability; the harness determines how effectively it uses context and tools.

lessons.point: Rare harmful actions make safety hard to benchmark with pass rates.
lessons.excerpt: That 1,001 time negates all the first thousand runs that went well.

entries.takeaway: Choose models for security work with your own task evaluations and a defined failure budget; leaderboards are only a shortlist.

actionable.title: Build a small in-house evaluation before picking a security model
actionable.detail: Start from the tasks and the failures you cannot accept, build a test set from your own code and workflows, and run shortlisted models through your actual harness, repeating runs to catch rare harmful actions.

entries.verify_note: Verifier refuted 'interviewees agree public rankings only shortlist candidates' (one Sonar quote) and 'harness matters as much as the model' (Dream's view alone); Sonar's leaderboard measures quality and security, not secure generation only.
entries.prior_art: The pool already holds claims that benchmark scores do not transfer to production tasks; this piece collects practitioner views without new data.

entries.title: Bound-conditioned latent inference cuts progressive image codec BD-rate on Kodak
entries.summary: Progressive image codecs send one bitstream that can be cut short at any point, encoding latents as trit-planes (base-3 digit layers). This NeurIPS 2026 paper treats the trits decoded so far as lower and upper bounds on each continuous latent, and uses the center and width of those bounds to refine both the entropy model and the reconstruction. On Kodak it lowers BD-rate (the average bitrate saving at equal quality) by 17.78% vs DPICT and 7.96% vs CTC, using one shared model instead of per-plane predictors.

lessons.point: Decoded trits are used as interval constraints on continuous latents, not only as discrete symbols.
lessons.excerpt: reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints

lessons.point: The method beats prior progressive codecs on rate-distortion on Kodak.
lessons.excerpt: reducing BD-rate by 17.78%over DPICT and by 7.96%over CTC on Kodak

lessons.point: One shared model replaces plane-specific predictors, cutting parameters and latency.
lessons.excerpt: replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about 5.3×fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC

entries.takeaway: A solid image-compression result, but it has no bearing on securing or building AI agents and harnesses.

actionable.title: No action for security or harness practitioners
actionable.detail: Only relevant if you ship learned image codecs: compare BLI against CTC/DPICT on your own rate-distortion and latency budget. Otherwise skip.

entries.prior_art: Builds directly on the DPICT and CTC trit-plane progressive codecs it benchmarks against; no related entry exists in the tracker. Verifier: DPICT (Lee et al., CVPR 2022) and CTC (Jeon et al., CVPR 2023) trit-plane progressive codecs, which BLI directly extends by treating decoded trits as interval bounds.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.

entries.title: PRISM benchmark shows pathology model calibration breaks down with scarce labels
entries.summary: PRISM tests eight pathology foundation models on six tile-level datasets, with label budgets from 1% to 100% and transfer between hospitals, and measures calibration (whether confidence matches accuracy). At 1% labels the link between accuracy rank and calibration rank becomes dataset-specific, and when transfer is weak, extra labels often make calibration error worse. Temperature scaling, a standard calibration fix, failed in 49 of 288 cells.

lessons.point: A model's accuracy ranking stops predicting its calibration ranking when labels are scarce.
lessons.excerpt: whereas at 1% labels the relationship becomes dataset-specific (rho = -0.24, I^2 = 67%)

lessons.point: When transfer to a new site is weak, more source-domain labels can make target calibration worse.
lessons.excerpt: below a transfer AUROC of roughly 0.85, more labels worsen target ECE in 86-88% of combinations

lessons.point: Post-hoc temperature scaling is not a reliable calibration fix.
lessons.excerpt: Temperature scaling fails to reduce ECE in 49 of 288 cells

entries.takeaway: Medical ML result, off-thesis here: the general point is not to treat an accuracy leaderboard as a stand-in for calibration under low labels or domain shift.

actionable.title: Measure calibration separately at your real label budget
actionable.detail: When choosing a foundation model for a task with few labels, report calibration error at your actual label fraction and on an out-of-distribution split. Do not assume a temperature fitted on source data will transfer.

entries.prior_art: No close entries; eval entries such as DecisionPivot (accuracy-matched routers diverge) share the theme that one headline metric hides reliability gaps.

entries.title: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro nears frontier scores, with open weights promised
entries.summary: Moonshot released Kimi K3.1 Pro on its API. It promises open weights by Nov 4, 2026, and offers a "Highspeed" tier that runs 2-3x faster at twice the price. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Artificial Analysis scored it 55, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 at 58.

lessons.point: The Highspeed tier doubles the price but keeps cache-hit input at the same price, so cache-heavy workloads lose less by choosing speed.
lessons.excerpt: They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same).

lessons.point: Its list price matches GPT-6.1 Sol and is half that of Claude Opus 5.5.
lessons.excerpt: $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.

lessons.point: Willison says a soon-to-be open-weight model has never before scored this close to the frontier.
lessons.excerpt: This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier.

lessons.point: Generic OpenAI-compatible endpoint runners may not log outputs, so you have to capture stdout and stderr yourself to keep reasoning traces.
lessons.excerpt: can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace).

actionable.title: Benchmark Kimi K3.1 Pro on your own harness tasks
actionable.detail: Run your existing agent eval suite against kimi-k3.1-pro through the OpenAI-compatible Moonshot endpoint at low, medium and max reasoning effort. Compare cost per solved task with your current model, and price the Highspeed tier against your cache-hit ratio. Recheck after the Nov 4 weights release if you plan to self-host.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: lessons are accurately attributed to Willison and Moonshot; the open-weights date is a promise and the price comparisons are Willison's, not independently checked.
entries.prior_art: Archive has Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence (tech report) and the Semgrep Kimi K3 code-security eval. This is an incremental release note with vendor and Artificial Analysis benchmark numbers.

entries.title: Hacker News developers describe fatigue from AI-era coding and agent review
entries.summary: In an Ask HN thread, developers describe fatigue in the AI era, including from running several agent workstreams at once and reviewing large amounts of generated code. Many say generated tests and pull requests go unreviewed, and AI code-review bots post comments too hard to verify. Coping tactics include agreeing intent and design up front, letting agents verify their own changes, mutation testing, and working in short single-stream loops.

lessons.point: Running four or five agent workstreams at once causes constant context switching and anxiety, even when output rises.
lessons.excerpt: I work on multple features (generally 4-5 work streams) concurrently, so am constantly context switching.

lessons.point: One commenter suggests mutation testing to find AI-written tests that cannot fail.
lessons.excerpt: Mutation testing (Stryker, mutmut, PIT) is how you find out which tests can’t fail.

lessons.point: Agreeing intent and design with the agent first cuts the workarounds that create review load.
lessons.excerpt: spending more time upfront working with agent on intent of the change, then design, so agent does not try to work around issues

lessons.point: Large AI-generated pull requests can ship without any human understanding them.
lessons.excerpt: So it ships having not had a single person understand what it does or was even for.

entries.takeaway: Human review capacity, not agent output, is now the bottleneck, so harnesses should cut what humans must read and prove that tests actually test something.

actionable.title: Gate AI-written tests with mutation testing
actionable.detail: Run a mutation tester (Stryker, mutmut or PIT) in CI on agent-generated tests. Reject test suites that leave mutants alive, so tests no one reviews still have to be able to fail.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: quotes supported; the title overstated parallel-agent review as the cause (commenters give varied reasons), retitled.
entries.prior_art: No close pool entry on developer fatigue. The tips repeat familiar advice on spec-first agent work and verification loops found across ai-research harness entries.
entries.author: mellosty

entries.title: RoboCasa-Shift shows equal success-rate drops in a VLA policy hide different failures
entries.summary: RoboCasa-Shift is a robustness benchmark for vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies. It pairs each clean rollout with a perturbed one that differs only in one shift, and records which task stage fails. Testing GR00T N1.5 over 1,040 rollouts, it finds that headline success rate hides a lot: one camera shift left success unchanged while 8 of 80 paired episodes flipped outcome, and two shifts with the same success drop failed at the first stage at very different rates (19.0% vs 36.4%).

lessons.point: Matched clean/perturbed pairs isolate the effect of one shift per comparison.
lessons.excerpt: matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift

lessons.point: Higher perturbation severity does not reliably mean worse performance, so severity sweeps need care.
lessons.excerpt: Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation.

lessons.point: The same aggregate drop can come from failures at different depths of execution.
lessons.excerpt: Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles.

entries.takeaway: Aggregate success rate can hide outcome flips and which task stage fails; the study covers one robot policy on four simulated tasks.

actionable.title: Report paired flip rates and stage of failure alongside success rate in long-horizon evals
actionable.detail: When testing an agent under a perturbation, run matched clean/perturbed pairs with the same seed and settings, count outcome flips in both directions (not just the net success delta), and log the first sub-step that failed so equal drops can be told apart.

entries.prior_art: Extends RoboCasa365 and general VLA robustness benchmarks that report aggregate task success; the eval-methodology point echoes the tracker claim that headline benchmark metrics can mask distinct failure modes. Verifier: Paired-outcome 'flip' analysis beyond aggregate accuracy (e.g., Dutta et al. 2024 'Accuracy is Not All You Need') plus VLA perturbation benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus/LIBERO-PRO; the stage-aware failure-depth breakdown is the incremental delta.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.

entries.title: Sebastian Raschka releases a from-scratch video course on building reasoning models

lessons.excerpt: The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools.

lessons.excerpt: Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU.

entries.title: alphaXiv says its 4B decision model nearly matches Jev except sarcasm
entries.summary: alphaXiv says it trained a 4-billion-parameter decision model on more than 117,000 decision-making examples using OpenResearch. It claims near-identical performance to Jev everywhere except sarcasm detection, and generalization to unseen tasks such as hate-speech severity. The post gives no benchmarks, numbers or methodology.

lessons.point: This is a claim of a small model distilled or trained for classification-style decisions.
lessons.excerpt: We trained a 4B decision model on over 117k decision-making examples with OpenResearch

lessons.point: The claimed parity has a named weak spot, sarcasm detection, and no supporting data.
lessons.excerpt: Our model performs practically identically to Jev in all areas except one: sarcasm detection

entries.takeaway: This is an unverified vendor claim, and small decision models still have to be benchmarked on your own data, as earlier pool entries showed.

actionable.title: Do not swap in claimed Jev-equivalents without your own eval
actionable.detail: If you consider this 4B model for routing or guardrail decisions, run it on contrast pairs from your own labeled set, DecisionPivot-style, and include sarcasm and other edge categories before replacing an existing judge.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: the lessons quote the post accurately, but the post itself gives no benchmark, metric or model details; low confidence reflects that.
entries.prior_art: Red Hat found Jev-style decision models not faster or more accurate than LLM-as-a-judge (ai-security). The DecisionPivot contrast-pair benchmark for decision models is in ai-research.

entries.title: Hugging Face launches an Open TTS Leaderboard ranking open text-to-speech models
entries.summary: Hugging Face built a TTS leaderboard that scores models with automatic metrics. Word error rate comes from an automatic speech recognition (ASR) model's transcript. Speaker-embedding similarity measures voice cloning, and real-time factor plus time-to-first-audio measure speed. This cuts evaluation from weeks of human voting to hours and covers open models that arena leaderboards mostly skip, but the metrics do not measure naturalness or listener preference, the authors say.

lessons.point: Automatic TTS metrics are proxies. Intelligibility and voice similarity scores say nothing about how natural or preferred the speech is, so they cannot replace human preference tests.
lessons.excerpt: Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference.

lessons.point: English scores do not predict quality in other languages. Evaluate each target language on its own.
lessons.excerpt: English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages.

lessons.point: For voice agents, measure time-to-first-audio. For non-streaming models this is the full generation time, which makes them slow for interactive use.
lessons.excerpt: For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier.

lessons.point: A simple latency benchmark rule: discard warm-up runs and report the median.
lessons.excerpt: We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

entries.takeaway: If you are choosing a TTS model for a voice agent, use this leaderboard to shortlist by error rate and time-to-first-audio, then listen to the outputs yourself before you decide.

actionable.title: Shortlist TTS models on objective metrics, then confirm by listening
actionable.detail: For a voice agent, filter the Open TTS Leaderboard by your target languages and the Streaming tab (time-to-first-audio at batch size 1, on your hardware class: GPU or CPU). Then use the Listen tab or your own prompts to check naturalness, since word error rate and speaker similarity do not measure it.

entries.prior_art: Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard; Seed-TTS-Eval and CV3-Eval benchmarks; TTS Arena v2 and Artificial Analysis TTS arena leaderboards. No closer entry in the corpus. Verifier's closest: Open ASR Leaderboard; TTS Arena v2; Seed-TTS-Eval.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: accurate; speech benchmark announcement with little value for harness builders.

entries.title: pi pod runs the pi coding agent in isolated sandboxes
entries.summary: pi pod is a new open-source project that runs sessions of the minimalist pi coding-agent harness inside isolated sandboxes on a server you control. The author argues that a minimal team agent environment needs four things: sandboxing, native clients, role-based access control (RBAC) for session sharing, and browser/native-app automation. The page is a launch announcement. It gives no details on how the isolation works and no security evaluation.

lessons.point: The project aims to keep the user's existing pi harness unchanged and add sandbox isolation around it.
lessons.excerpt: pi pod aims to seamlessly run your pi in an isolated sandbox with minimal, carefully curated tooling to get out the way and give you the boring stuff you need.

lessons.point: The author's view of the minimum team agent environment: sandboxing, native clients, RBAC session sharing, and browser and native-app automation.
lessons.excerpt: I consider agent sandboxing, native clients, rbac session sharing, and surface automation (namely browser and native apps) to comprise the minimal agentic engineering environment that should be used for software engineers in an organization.

lessons.point: Self-hosting is pitched as the way for companies to keep the whole agent environment in their own data center.
lessons.excerpt: Self-hosting also is a great option for businesses who want their entire agentic environment in their preferred data center.

entries.takeaway: Another self-hosted option for sandboxing coding agents, but the page gives no isolation details, so treat it as a lead to evaluate, not a proven security control.

actionable.title: Check pi pod's isolation model before you rely on it
actionable.detail: If you run pi for a team, read the pi-pod/pipod repository to find out what isolation backs each pod (container, gVisor, microVM), what outbound network access it allows, and how credentials reach the pod. Do this before you treat the sandbox as a security boundary.

entries.prior_art: Omnigent meta-harness with policy enforcement and sandboxing; OneCLI per-employee sandboxed agents; OpenAI Agents API hosted harness with a choice of sandbox (all in archive.json/ai-research.json). Verifier's closest: existing agent-sandbox wrappers (OneCLI, Omnigent).

entries.title: Anthropic staff, unlike most US adults, expect Nobel-level AI discovery by 2030
entries.summary: In August 2026 Anthropic surveyed a nationally representative sample of US adults and its own staff about AI capabilities, adoption, time savings and jobs. Staff expect much faster progress. On average they expect AI to be able to do 75% of their own work by 2030, against 28% for US workers. Both groups link expected exposure of their own job to higher unemployment forecasts at about the same rate.
entries.takeaway: This is an economics and public-opinion survey with little practical value for builders, though its one practical data point is that regular AI users at work rank data privacy and security as the top obstacle to adoption.

lessons.point: Staff and the public largely agree on current AI capability but diverge sharply on how fast it will progress.
lessons.excerpt: 39% of US adults and 91% of staff expect that AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030.

lessons.point: Self-reported time savings differ widely between the general workforce and staff at a frontier lab.
lessons.excerpt: Among US adults who use AI at work, 26% say a task takes a quarter of the time or less with AI, compared to 59% of Anthropic staff.

lessons.point: Among regular AI users at work, security and privacy concerns rank as the leading barrier to adoption.
lessons.excerpt: US adults who use AI regularly at work rank data privacy and security concerns first (42% consider it among the top three obstacles, compared with 37% among the rest)

entries.title: OpenAI proposes US-led international technical standards for frontier AI
entries.summary: OpenAI argues for US-led global technical standards for frontier AI, built through the network of national AI safety institutes and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). It says fully autonomous recursive self-improvement (RSI) is not happening today and should not be pursued until it can be done safely. Proposed standards cover measuring autonomous AI research, when automated research must trigger human review, and shared incident severity levels and reporting thresholds. The standards would not be licenses or prerelease approvals.

lessons.point: OpenAI states fully autonomous RSI is not happening yet and should wait until it can be done safely.
lessons.excerpt: Fully autonomous RSI is not happening today, and we should not pursue it unless and until it can be done safely.

lessons.point: Proposed standards include defining which automated research processes must trigger immediate human review.
lessons.excerpt: Human oversight over automated AI research, including what kinds of automated AI research processes should trigger immediate human review.

lessons.point: The proposal explicitly excludes licensing or mandatory prerelease approval.
lessons.excerpt: These technical standards would not be licenses, mandatory prerelease review, or approval requirements for AI models.

lessons.point: A stated motivation is that national evals and incident definitions could conflict and prevent comparison.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluations, reporting requirements, and incident definitions by different nations could conflict

entries.takeaway: A policy position with no technical content; useful only as a signal that incident severity levels and human-review triggers for automated research may become shared standards.

actionable.title: Track emerging incident-severity and human-review-trigger standards
actionable.detail: If you run autonomous agents that do research or code changes, watch CAISI / AI safety institute and Appia Foundation outputs for incident severity levels and reporting thresholds. Pre-define your own list of agent actions that require immediate human review, so you can map to these standards later.

entries.prior_art: External-testing commitments via UK AISI/US CAISI; no prior entry on recursive self-improvement standards.

entries.title: Riley Goodside mocks the claim that model collapse halted LLM progress
entries.summary: An X post by @goodside sarcastically claims that model collapse, from training on AI-generated web data, has stalled LLMs since 2023 and will make them disappear by 2030. It is satire of the model-collapse prediction, not evidence, and it contains no data.

lessons.point: The post satirizes the model-collapse prediction by claiming the opposite of the progress practitioners see.
lessons.excerpt: This is why LLMs have made no progress since that time, steadily declining on all benchmarks

lessons.point: The idea being mocked is that training on AI-generated web text degrades future models.
lessons.excerpt: training on poisoned internet data generated by AI

entries.takeaway: A joke, not a finding, and it signals only that practitioners see model collapse as an overblown prediction so far.

actionable.title: Treat model-collapse claims as unproven in either direction
actionable.detail: Do not cite this post as evidence. If synthetic-data contamination matters to your pipeline, measure it directly on your own data instead of relying on social-media takes.
